# Citi Bike riders urge for $3 fee cap as transportation costs rise
August 31, 2026

New York City cyclists and transit advocates are pushing for a $3 cap on Citi Bike rides as prices continue to rise. The campaign, launched by the nonprofit Transportation Alternatives, seeks to limit what Citi Bike members pay for a 45-minute e-bike ride.
Citi Bike is currently owned by Lyft and does not receive subsidies from the city. Transportation Alternatives has noted that Lyft’s bike-share programs in other cities offer lower prices because of the public subsidies provided.

“Most every other bike share system in North America and definitely across the world is paid for by some combination of riders and public subsidy,” Ben Furnas, executive director of Transportation Alternatives, told AMNY. “There’s no reason why New York shouldn’t be similar. And we could have a bike share system that’s much less expensive.”
The Department of Transportation currently has a contract with Lyft, allowing the company to raise Citi Bike prices. DOT could negotiate for a price cap when the agreement expires in 2029.
City Council member Lincoln Restler is now sponsoring a bill that would update the contract to and cap the cost of one-hour e-bike rides at $3 for Citi Bike members, matching the subway fare. Although he originally introduced this bill in 2024, it was not able to move forward because of opposition from former Mayor Eric Adams’ administration.
However, subsidies from the city alone may not be enough to lower Citi Bike prices. In the past, Lyft has reported a small profit from Citi Bike after years of deficits, with a lot of its operating costs going towards its system maintenance, including moving bikes and changing e-bike batteries.

Despite this, Restler noted that rising operating costs can be prevented by using the city subsidies to improve Citi Bike operations instead, which could make the system cheaper and more efficient.

Council Member Lincoln Restler introduced a bill in September 2024 (Int. 1039-2024) that would cap a member’s Citi Bike ride at the subway fare, now $3, for e-bike trips under an hour and classic trips under two.
New York gives Lyft public space, no competition and automatic price increases. In exchange, nothing about Citi Bike’s finances should be opaque.
The State Comptroller audited DOT’s oversight of the contract last December and called it “passive.” DOT does no calculations of its own to verify what Lyft reports. In twelve years, no published audit (2021, 2023, 2025) has examined the expense side of Citi Bike, the side that justifies the price. The contract itself is part of the problem. Written in 2014, before e-bikes existed, it lets member prices rise every year by inflation plus two percentage points, automatically, with no city sign-off. Non-member prices have no cap at all.
E-bike minutes are 40 percent of Citi Bike’s revenue, and a cap that low would wipe out much of it. The city would have to make up the difference with a subsidy, likely tens of millions of dollars a year. But, how do you size a subsidy for a program whose true costs nobody outside Lyft has seen?
